newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judge ends plane bomb probe, targets Libya.
newsitem.headline: French judge ends plane bomb probe, targets Libya.

text.p: France's chief anti-terrorism investigator ended on Tuesday a probe into the 1989 bombing of a French airliner over the Sahara and urged that six Libyans including a brother-in-law of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi be put on trial, justice sources said.

The sources said that more than seven years after the UTA airlines DC-10 crashed in the Sahara desert, killing all 170 people on board, Judge Jean-Louis Bruguiere had concluded that the order to blow up the plane came from the brother-in-law, Abdallah Senoussi.
The judge's investigation was sent to public prosecutors on Tuesday, the sources said. But a trial before a French criminal court court was unlikely before late this year or early 1998, they said.

Gaddafi had allowed Bruguiere to question some 50 members of the Libyan intelligence services in Tripoli in July 1996, during a visit in which the judge also seized a U.S.-made Samsonite suitcase he found in intelligence service offices.
Investigators believe the suitcase is identical to one packed with explosives and used to bring down the plane.
The sources said Bruguiere also found timers and detonators similar to those believed used in the bombing when he searched the Libyan intelligence offices.

In facilitating the judge's probe, Gaddafi effectively abandoned the intelligence officers in an attempt at reconciliation after the U.N. slapped economic sanctions on Tripoli following the UTA crash and that of a Pan Am flight over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988.
"The clear conclusion is that the bombing was ordered by Senoussi. France was an enemy of Libyan expansionism at the time," a source close to the probe said.
The source said the probe, carried out in cooperation with the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), had ruled out any non-Libyan involvement.
"The most likely scenario is that Gaddafi did not know about the bombing before it happened, and that officials acted following his general policy statements," the source said.
The bombing occurred at the height of tension between France and Libya over Chad, where the two countries' forces clashed repeatedly in the 1970s and 1980s.

The accused include Senoussi, the number two in Libya's foreign intelligence service at the time, Abdallah Elazragh, a diplomat then working in Brazzaville, and Abdesslam Issa Shibani, a colonel in charge of technical services at Libyan intelligence.

Also accused of murder, destruction with the use of explosives and conspiracy are Abdesslam Hamouda, suspected of buying a timer for the bomb in Germany, and alleged secret agents Ibrahim Naeli and Musbah Arbas.

The sources said it was unlikely that Gaddafi would hand over the accused, but that pressure may be brought to bear on Tripoli to jail them in Libya if they are found guilty, or to eventually pay compensation to the families of the victims.

The families of French victims of the bombing have, under French provisions, been given some 800,000 francs ($140,000) each in compensation, but the families of British and American victims have yet to receive funds.
Following the judge's visit to Tripoli, Libyan authorities sent him three heavy files of judicial proceedings including minutes of witness questioning and material evidence.
Investigators picked some four to five million parts of the downed airliner from the desert sands and rebuilt up to 85 percent of the original plane in a Paris hangar.

They worked out to within a square metre where the bomb went off in the forward cargo loading bay. The reconstruction was studied by investigators probing the crash of TWA Flight 800 off Long Island last July.
